rules.section: 3. Tests, and showing how each item is tested
3. Tests, and showing how each item is tested
3. Tests, and showing how each item is tested

judged.title: One sentence on what the crate is for
judged.text: 1. **One sentence on what the crate is for**, then a runnable example of its central use. [judged]

judged.title: Overview
judged.text: 2. **Overview:** the main types and functions, each linked, and the invariants they keep. A table works well for a crate of modules. [judged]

judged.title: A map of the rest of the page
judged.text: 3. **A map of the rest of the page**, with links to its sections. [judged]

judged.title: Examples
judged.text: 4. **Examples:** a cookbook of `## Example: <what it does>` blocks. They show edge cases and failures, not only the happy path: a rejected input, a boundary, a cycle, saturation. [judged]

judged.title: Why this crate?
judged.text: 5. **Why this crate?** What it does that a general-purpose crate would get wrong for this use. Say why, concretely. [judged]

judged.title: Related crates
judged.text: 6. **Related crates:** a table of crates doing similar jobs. Give the version checked and why this crate takes another approach. [judged] Every claim rests on a check that was actually run: an input tried, a root compared. A crate adopted rather than reimplemented is named too, as something this one builds on.

judged.title: Crate features
judged.text: 7. **Crate features:** every feature, or "None", said plainly. [judged]

judged.title: Minimum Rust version
judged.text: 8. **Minimum Rust version:** the `rust-version`, and the policy. It may rise in a release that bumps the second number (`y` in `x.y.z`, and in `0.y.z`), never in one that bumps only the third. [judged]

judged.title: Versioning
judged.text: 9. **Versioning:** Cargo's convention, and that the public API is checked against the last release. [judged]

judged.title: Examples use `?`, with the error plumbing hidden
judged.text: - Examples use `?`, with the error plumbing hidden: `# Ok::<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>>(())`. [judged]

judged.title: Hidden setup lines (`# let ...`) are used sparingly
judged.text: - Hidden setup lines (`# let ...`) are used sparingly. A reader must be able to tell where every name in a visible example comes from. [judged]

judged.title: `# Errors`
judged.text: - **`# Errors`** says exactly when an error happens. Where that is a promise, it is part of the semver contract, so word it as one: "fails only if...". [judged]

judged.title: `# Panics`
judged.text: - **`# Panics`** wherever something can panic. [judged]

judged.title: Domain sections where they matter
judged.text: - Domain sections where they matter: `# Complexity` for traversals and proofs, `# Platform behavior` when results could differ. [judged]

judged.title: Public error types are `#[non_exhaustive]`, or opaque structs with a `kind()`
judged.text: - Public error types are `#[non_exhaustive]`, or opaque structs with a `kind()`. An enum left exhaustive says why in its docs. [judged]

judged.title: Types of values that come from someone else (sizes, indexes and lengths read from the wire or a peer) do not depend on the target's word size
judged.text: - Types of values that come from someone else (sizes, indexes and lengths read from the wire or a peer) do not depend on the target's word size. Use `u64`, not `usize`, so a 32-bit or `wasm32` machine can check anything a 64-bit one can. Use `usize` only for what indexes this machine's memory. [judged]

judged.section: 3. Tests, and showing how each item is tested
judged.title: Test vectors from independent sources
judged.question: are the sources really independent?
judged.text: - **Test vectors from independent sources** live in `testdata/` as JSON: RFCs, other implementations, published test suites. Every case names its source. They are read by `tests/vectors.rs`, and regenerated and compared in CI (`make vectors-check`). [checked: RS-TEST-01, make vectors-check, pubkit conform; judged: are the sources really independent?]

judged.section: 3. Tests, and showing how each item is tested
judged.title: Property tests
judged.text: - **Property tests** (proptest) cover invariants over many inputs: round-trips, and consistency at random sizes. [judged]

judged.section: 3. Tests, and showing how each item is tested
judged.title: Oracles
judged.text: - **Oracles:** where an established crate implements the same standard, its results are compared with ours in the tests. It is a dev-dependency only. [judged]

judged.section: 3. Tests, and showing how each item is tested
judged.title: Every test says what it covers
judged.question: is the claim true?
judged.text: - **Every test says what it covers** with a `// covers: module::item` comment. A test claims only items in its own module's area. [checked: RS-TEST-02, make doc-coverage-check, library; the guard fails on a name that does not exist; judged: is the claim true?]

judged.title: Every function that parses or verifies something from outside (bytes, text, proofs, signatures) has a cargo-fuzz target in `fuzz/`
judged.question: is any entry point missing a target?
judged.text: - Every function that parses or verifies something from outside (bytes, text, proofs, signatures) has a **cargo-fuzz target** in `fuzz/`. [judged: is any entry point missing a target?]

judged.title: `Cargo.toml` states
judged.text: - `Cargo.toml` states: - `description`, `license`, `repository`, `documentation`, `keywords` and `categories`; - an explicit `include` list; - `rust-version`; - `[package.metadata.docs.rs]` with `all-features = true` and `rustdoc-args = ["--generate-link-to-definition"]`. [judged]

judged.title: The `include` patterns are anchored with `/` (`"/README.md"`, `"/src/**/*.rs"`)
judged.text: - The `include` patterns are anchored with `/` (`"/README.md"`, `"/src/**/*.rs"`). Cargo reads them like gitignore patterns, so a bare `README.md` or `LICENSE` also matches any file of that name below, such as one in a Python test environment. `cargo package --list` shows exactly what ships. [judged]

judged.title: `make publish-check` runs `cargo publish --dry-run --locked` with a target directory of its own (`CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target/publish-check`)
judged.text: - `make publish-check` runs `cargo publish --dry-run --locked` with a target directory of its own (`CARGO_TARGET_DIR=target/publish-check`). If the verify build shares `target/`, its dep-info names the packaged copy's sources. After that, cargo reports the crate up to date however `src/` changes, so tests run a stale binary. [judged]

judged.title: Docs build as docs.rs builds them
judged.question: run it before each release
judged.text: - **Docs build as docs.rs builds them.** That means from the packaged crate, on nightly, with `--cfg docsrs` and the metadata's flags, with no warnings. [judged: run it before each release]

judged.title: The README is short and different from the crate docs
judged.text: - The **README** is short and different from the crate docs: - a Documentation link that says what the docs cover; - Usage; - one example; - Minimum Rust version; - Security: how to report, and where the checks are described. [judged]

judged.title: `SECURITY.md`
judged.text: - **`SECURITY.md`** says how to report a vulnerability (private reporting), what is checked and when, and what fuzzing has found. [judged] Every repository has one. [checked: RS-SUP-04, pubkit conform]

judged.title: Its documentation is its README and its `--help`
judged.text: - **Its documentation is its README and its `--help`.** docs.rs renders no pages for a binary-only crate. The README carries what section 1 puts in the crate root: - what the tool is for, and its central use as a runnable command; - an overview of its commands; - why this tool; - related tools; - installation; - Minimum Rust version; - versioning. `--help` names every command and flag, and the README agrees with it. [judged]

judged.title: Module docs still matter
judged.text: - **Module docs still matter.** `//!` docs on `main.rs` and each module say what it does and why, for whoever maintains it. Section 2's rules apply to anything `pub` that another module relies on, with these changes: - `#![deny(missing_docs)]` checks nothing in a binary, because nothing is exported. Find undocumented items with `cargo clippy -- -W clippy::missing_docs_in_private_items`. - Doctests do not run in a binary target, so section 2's example rule does not apply. The README's example commands and the functional scenarios take their place. [judged]

judged.title: Its versioned interface is what users depend on
judged.text: - **Its versioned interface is what users depend on:** - commands and flags; - exit codes; - output meant for scripts; - the configuration files it reads. The README or a dedicated document names that interface. A change to it is recorded as `changed` or `removed`, like an API break. cargo-semver-checks does not apply, because there is no library API. [judged]

judged.title: Its behaviour is tested end to end
judged.text: - **Its behaviour is tested end to end.** That means a functional suite (pubkit's Gherkin plugin) that runs the built binary as a user would, in addition to unit tests. [judged]

judged.title: Its usage text is documentation
judged.text: - **Its usage text is documentation.** The `--help` output, usually a string constant, is held to the same standard as the README. `--help` exits 0 and prints to stdout. [judged]

judged.title: Metadata
judged.text: - **Metadata:** `documentation` points at the README in the repository. `[package.metadata.docs.rs]` is not needed, since docs.rs renders no pages for a binary. [judged]

judged.title: `// covers:` comments
judged.text: - **`// covers:` comments** may name module-private items by their module path (`api::allowed`). `TESTING.md` and the doc-coverage guard are for libraries, and are not required of a binary. [judged]

judged.title: Related tools
judged.text: - **Related tools** may include tools that are not Rust crates. Name the version or date checked, and how: their documentation, their source, or a run. [judged]

judged.title: Writing
judged.text: - Plain, specific sentences. Say what something does and why. No marketing, no "simply" or "just", no claims nobody checked. - One idea per sentence. If a sentence needs a semicolon to carry two, split it. - Name things exactly: the type, the function, the RFC section. - Never describe something that is planned as done.
